preamble.summary: LXX Joel's central importance for the NT is concentrated in the Spirit-poured-out prophecy of 2:28–32 (LXX and English; = MT 3:1–5). Peter's Pentecost sermon at Acts 2:17–21 cites this passage at length in its LXX form, identifying the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh as fulfilled that morning in Jerusalem. Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5), 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved,' is independently cited at Romans 10:13 as a universalizing soteriological formula.
preamble.notable_variants: Versification: MT Joel 3–4 = LXX (and English) Joel 2:28–3:21. The LXX preserves the Hebrew chapter numbering. The 'all flesh' (pasa sarx) universal scope at 2:28 that Acts 2 makes the hermeneutic key to post-Pentecost ecclesiology.
preamble.theological_legacy: Joel 2:28–32 in its LXX form is, arguably, the NT's most formally cited OT passage — quoted block-by-block in the sermon that launches the Christian movement. The LXX's 'all flesh' is what makes Peter's argument possible: the Spirit poured out 'on all flesh' can include Jews and Gentiles, men and women, young and old, slave and free.

renderings.lxx_reading: ἐκχεῶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός μου ἐπὶ πᾶσαν σάρκα
renderings.mt_rendering: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
renderings.lxx_rendering: I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh
notes: Acts 2:17 quotes this verse in its LXX form with one important adjustment: Peter adds 'in the last days' (en tais eschatais hēmerais) — a phrase not present in either MT or LXX Joel — and uses the LXX's 'from my Spirit' (apo tou pneumatos mou) rather than the Hebrew's direct 'my Spirit.'

The LXX's partitive apo ('from') at 'from my Spirit' is theologically consequential: the Spirit is not diminished by being poured out on many; each recipient receives from the one Spirit without depleting the source. This supplied patristic trinitarian theology with a useful grammatical nuance.
Peter's whole Pentecost sermon reads Joel 2:28–32 as fulfilled in the events of the morning. The argument requires the LXX's specific vocabulary at every turn.

renderings.lxx_reading: πᾶς ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται
renderings.mt_rendering: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved
renderings.lxx_rendering: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved
notes: Romans 10:13 quotes this verse verbatim in its LXX form — pas gar hos an epikalesētai to onoma kyriou sōthēsetai — as the climactic scriptural warrant for Paul's argument that 'there is no distinction between Jew and Greek: the same Lord is Lord of all.'
Peter cites the same verse at Acts 2:21, concluding his Joel-quotation with it.

The LXX's Pas ('everyone') and the universal-access reading are what Paul and Luke press: the 'everyone' is the textual lever for universalizing the Hebrew Bible's 'call on the name of the Lord' from an Israelite covenant-call into a Gentile-admitting salvific formula.

The LXX's kyrios for Hebrew YHWH is the identification that lets Paul apply the verse Christologically: Romans 10:13's kyrios IS Jesus (per 10:9, 'confess Jesus as Lord'). The LXX's divine-name rendering supplies the Christological pivot.
